name: Timor-Leste
headline: Timor-Leste is in Tier 1 (convergence) of the 28 August regional snapshot: El Niño is expected to reduce seasonal rainfall from November 2026 to April 2027, and parts of the centre and east were already 30–50% below average in late July–August. In mid-October transboundary haze pushed Dili's AQI to 165–174 and the Government suspended face-to-face classes nationwide for 15–17 October. The risk falls on a population where 45% of under-fives are stunted and 27% (360,097 people) were in IPC Phase 3 or above during the 2023–24 El Niño, although food prices were still in deflation in August 2026 (−0.60% year on year).

hazard_outlook.text: Below-normal rainfall most likely (SEA RCC Network, issued 1 Aug); near-normal temperatures at the southern edge of ASMC's outlook. The 28 Aug FAO/WFP/UN Women/WMO/OCHA snapshot rates climate concern very high — drier.

Main risk is a delayed October wet-season onset disrupting rice and maize planting; August–September heat raises fire risk to coffee plantations and free-grazing livestock (FAO/WFP/UN Women/WMO/OCHA snapshot, 28 Aug 2026). DNMG warned haze concentrations could rise again depending on smoke transport (Government of Timor-Leste, 14 Oct 2026).

Reduced seasonal rainfall, with possible extreme drought and heat, water shortages, erratic rainfall and reduced agricultural production (UNICEF Timor-Leste, 1 Sep 2026; Government of Timor-Leste, 15 Oct 2026). UNDP hazard mapping concentrates moderate to severe drought in the south and east (UNDP Timor-Leste, 4 Aug 2026).
Below-average rainy season for Timor-Leste, with dry conditions possibly persisting into 2027 (regional reading cited in the wiki; issuing agency not named).

points: Transboundary smoke from fires in the region pushed Dili's AQI to 165–174, classed as harmful to health (Government of Timor-Leste, 14 Oct 2026).
Dili residents reported pollution had been worse earlier in the week of 12 October, with smoke covering the city and surrounding mountains (AFP, 15 Oct 2026).
Unhealthy air persisted across Timor-Leste including Dili on 16–17 October (The Star/AFP, 17 Oct 2026).
Face-to-face teaching was suspended for 15–17 October throughout the national territory, from pre-school to senior secondary and vocational schools (Government of Timor-Leste, 14 Oct 2026).
Schools were required to provide home-study guidance and draw up plans to recover lost teaching and learning (Government of Timor-Leste, 14 Oct 2026).

Rainfall stayed below the 1991–2020 average across the country from 27 July to 26 August 2026, and only ~0–2 mm was forecast for most of the country for 14–22 September (UNICEF Timor-Leste StoryMap, data to mid-Sep 2026).

In the 2022 Census, households reporting insufficient drinking water were highest in Passabe (88.1%), Lequidoe (80.5%), Bobonaro (77.6%), Oesilo (77.4%) and Remexio (76.6%) (UNICEF Timor-Leste StoryMap, 7 Aug 2026).
Over one third of households lack an adequate water source (IPC, 29 Feb 2024).
45% of children under five are stunted; drought can deepen this through poor diets, water- and sanitation-related illness and weaker access to services (UNICEF Timor-Leste StoryMap, 7 Aug 2026).
UNICEF flags Aileu Vila, Hatulia, Ermera, Maubisse and Bazartete as high dryness–high child population hotspots (UNICEF Timor-Leste StoryMap, 7 Aug 2026).

A delayed October wet-season onset would disrupt rice and maize planting, and August–September heat raises fire risk to coffee plantations and free-grazing livestock (FAO/WFP/UN Women/WMO/OCHA snapshot, 28 Aug 2026).
Moderate to severe drought conditions are mapped in the southern and eastern parts of the country (UNDP Timor-Leste, 4 Aug 2026).
Food inflation was −0.60% year on year in August 2026; diesel was unchanged against February and gasoline +10.64% (WFP monthly data, August) (WFP Asia-Pacific, 5 Oct 2026).
Headline CPI rose +0.2% from February to June 2026 (WFP Asia-Pacific, 7 Aug 2026).

The Petroleum Fund stands at about $26 billion, Bayu-Undan ceased production in 2025, and the IMF warned in 2025 the fund could be depleted by 2038; Greater Sunrise first production is put at 2034–2035 (ABC News, 18 Oct 2026).
Drought increases pressure on women and girls to fetch water, and household stress raises risks of school dropout, child abuse and child labour (UNICEF Timor-Leste StoryMap, 7 Aug 2026).

The Minister of the Interior opened a National Workshop on El Niño Preparedness in Dili on 9 October 2026, with the Secretariat of State for Civil Protection, the Civil Protection Authority and UNDP (Government of Timor-Leste, 15 Oct 2026).

The Secretary of State for Civil Protection set out anticipatory actions and early-warning mechanisms, community information campaigns, food and water conservation, and awareness to avoid bush burning and tree felling (Government of Timor-Leste, 15 Oct 2026).

The Government suspended classes nationwide for 15–17 October and advised households to keep children indoors, use respiratory protection, keep windows closed and avoid burning waste (Government of Timor-Leste, 14 Oct 2026).
Timor-Leste capped fuel prices following the Middle East crisis (FAO/OCHA/WMO/WFP snapshot, 17 Jun 2026).

UNICEF calls for preparedness in October–December 2026 in the highest-risk municipalities, including safe water storage, school water monitoring, nutrition screening, disease monitoring and ORS preparation (UNICEF Timor-Leste, 1 Sep 2026).
UNICEF's subnational Children's Climate Risk Index and Disaster Risk Model is being implemented in Timor-Leste among eight countries in the region (UNICEF EAPRO, 30 Jun 2026).
Cruz Vermelha de Timor-Leste and Palang Merah Indonesia planned joint cross-border drought assessments by July under an existing MoU (IFRC, 6 Jul 2026).
Timor-Leste is one of four Asia-Pacific priority countries in the FAO–WFP anticipatory-action appeal of US$202 million for 8.8 million people in 22 countries (FAO–WFP, 18 Jun 2026).
Timor-Leste is one of only two Asia-Pacific countries running FAO's Combined Drought Index as an operational anticipatory-action trigger, with PNG (FAO/OCHA/WMO/WFP snapshot, 17 Jun 2026).

CERF sets the action window for Timor-Leste drought at prepositioning before November 2026, and lists Timor-Leste among eleven recurring-vulnerability countries for possible non-framework support (CERF secretariat, 30 Jun 2026).

history: 2015–16: El Niño drought was felt most acutely in Covalima, Oecusse, Baucau, Viqueque and Lautem, affecting around 400,000 people (OCHA ROAP, 20 May 2026); national maize and rice production fell substantially (UNICEF Timor-Leste StoryMap, 2026). CERF allocated US$800,000 for drought (CERF secretariat, 30 Jun 2026).

2023–24: the IPC placed 27% of the population (360,097 people) in Phase 3 or above for Nov 2023 – Apr 2024 and projected 363,997 for May – Sep 2024, with Phase 4 rising from 18,592 to 22,278; twelve of fourteen municipalities were in Phase 3, deepest in Ermera (50%), Covalima (45%) and Ainaro (40%) (IPC, 29 Feb 2024).

2023–24: the Combined Drought Index showed drought-like conditions in every municipality in November 2023, and the CPI reached 124.7 in December 2023, the highest since 2013 (IPC, 29 Feb 2024); CERF allocated US$2,076,861 for drought response (CERF secretariat, 30 Jun 2026).
Across eight El Niño events paired with positive IODs (1982/83–2023/24), Timor-Leste ranks very high for below-average rainfall response (FAO/WFP/UN Women/WMO/OCHA snapshot, 28 Aug 2026).
cautions: Fuel price readings disagree: the 28 Aug snapshot gives diesel ~+27% and gasoline ~+39% since the crisis began, while WFP's October issue (WFP monthly data, August vs February) gives diesel 0.00% and gasoline +10.64%; the June snapshot records that Timor-Leste capped fuel prices.

Rainy-season timing differs across sources: reduced rainfall November 2026 – April 2027 (UNICEF; Government), a delayed October onset (28 Aug snapshot) and a below-average December–May rainy season (regional reading whose issuing agency the wiki does not name).

UNICEF cautions that one dry month is not a drought, that El Niño does not automatically produce drought countrywide, and that its hotspot map shows exposure, not observed impact, vulnerability or coping capacity.

The IPC 2023–24 Phase 3+ figure is not necessarily the full population needing urgent action, drought was never officially declared, and the latest official data on malnutrition, water access, agricultural production and household expenditure were unavailable to the analysts; the release notes marginal rounding inconsistencies (Phase 4 shown as about 19,000 and 18,500 against a table value of 18,592).
Ranking lists diverge: Timor-Leste is Tier 1 in the 28 Aug FAO/WFP/UN Women/WMO/OCHA snapshot but only in the Monitoring tier of the IASC ENSO Cell, which weights existing caseloads and fragility.
